Primer 1 left you with vectors. Stand several of them side by side, all the
same length, and you have a rectangle.

That rectangle is what you analyse. **One row per observation**: a person, a
household, a notification. **One column per variable**. In the tidyverse the
rectangle is called a **tibble**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run the cells from the top.** The first one builds the data that all the
others use. If a later cell says `object not found`, you have skipped it.
:::


## Building a tibble

`tibble()` takes named vectors and lines them up as columns. Each one must be
the same length.

```{webr}
library(tibble)

participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

participants
```

Read the header it printed. `# A tibble: 5 × 5` means 5 rows by 5 columns.

Under each column name sits its type. `<chr>` is text. `<dbl>` is a number with
decimals. `<lgl>` is `TRUE`/`FALSE`. A plain `data.frame` tells you none of that
until you ask.

::: {.callout-note}
## Know what one row represents
Many "how do I do X in R" problems turn out to be data in the wrong shape. If a person appears on 3 rows because they had 3 visits, the observation
is a *visit*, not a person. That is fine, as long as you know it and say it.
Confusion starts when you cannot say what one row is.
:::

## Looking at one

4 functions. Use them on every dataset you open, before anything else.

```{webr}
nrow(participants)      # how many rows
ncol(participants)      # how many columns
names(participants)     # what the columns are called
str(participants)       # types and the first few values
```

`summary()` is the fifth, and it is worth the extra second:

```{webr}
summary(participants)
```

A minimum age of 3, or a blood pressure of 0, shows up here and nowhere else
until it has already ruined an analysis.

## Getting a column out

`$` unwraps one column back into the vector it was.

```{webr}
participants$age
mean(participants$sbp)
```

That is the pattern: a tibble is a bundle of vectors, and `$` gets one.

Everything you learned in Primer 1 now applies to a real dataset:

```{webr}
# What proportion are smokers? A logical column sums as 1s and 0s.
mean(participants$smoker)

# How many have systolic BP of 140 or more?
sum(participants$sbp >= 140)
```

## Counting a categorical variable

`table()` is base R and it is still the fastest way to see what is in a column.

```{webr}
table(participants$district)
```

Cross two columns and you have the beginning of a 2×2 table, which is where
Primer 7 starts:

```{webr}
table(participants$smoker, participants$sbp >= 140)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `table()` drops missing values silently
By default `table()` does not count `NA`s and does not tell you it left them
out. Your percentages then quietly refer to a smaller denominator than you
think. Use `table(x, useNA = "ifany")` whenever the column might have holes.
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Build a tibble from named, equal-length vectors.
- Say what one row of any dataset represents, before you analyse it.
- Look at a new dataset with `nrow`, `names`, `str` and `summary`.
- Pull a column out with `$` and use everything from Primer 1 on it.
- Count categories with `table()`, and remember that it hides `NA` by default.
- See why an overall proportion is not the average of group proportions.
